entry.evidence: the controls on the export of DSi to the North Atlantic is lacking

steps.action: Pose the question of what controls the export of riverine and other Arctic DSi through Fram Strait, given that most riverine DSi is not consumed.
steps.quote: the controlling processes of this remain unclear

steps.action: Take rival explanations of the heavy Arctic δ30Si signature from the literature: physical processes, biological modification in surface waters, and productivity plus biogenic Si burial of riverine DSi.
steps.quote: This heavy isotopic enrichment is attributed to physical processes (Liguori et al., 2020) and biological modification within surface waters

steps.action: Sample nutrients and isotopes on two 2018 Fram Strait CTD sections (spring and late summer) and on Ile-de-France profiles from 2017 to 2019.
steps.quote: Samples were collected from two CTD sections across the Fram Strait (JR17005 and FS2018) and from CTD profiles near the Ile-de-France between 2017–2019

steps.action: Check that freezing did not bias the DSi concentrations by re-measuring acid-preserved isotope samples with the HACH reagent method, and compare against the other cruise and the literature.
steps.quote: Both datasets from frozen and acidified were in very good agreement

steps.action: Adapt the MAGIC co-precipitation protocol and cation-exchange purification so that δ30Si can be measured by MC-ICP-MS at DSi below 10 µM.
steps.quote: were adapted to allow measurements at concentrations below 10 µ M

steps.action: Characterize the adapted method against international and seawater standards compared with inter-laboratory values, and against duplicate seawater samples run in separate sessions.
steps.quote: The mean absolute difference between duplicate samples analysed was ± 0.04 ‰ (1 SD).

steps.action: Report hydrography, nutrient concentrations, N*, Si* and isotope signatures by water mass: PSW is higher in DSi and heavier in δ30Si than AW, enriched in δ15N and lighter in δ18O.
steps.quote: DSi in PSW was isotopically heavier than DSi in AW ( p < 0.02 )

steps.action: Compare the AW and PSW δ30Si values with published North Atlantic, Canadian Basin and transpolar drift measurements.
steps.quote: This is comparable to measurements of the upper halocline layer in the Canadian Basin

steps.action: Check the accuracy of the nitrate isotope measurements against the profiles published by Tuerena et al. (2021a).
steps.quote: the dataset aligns and follow the same trends as profiles reported in Tuerena et al. (2021a)

steps.action: Set out the closed- and open-system Rayleigh fractionation expectations for nitrate and DSi uptake as reference curves.
steps.quote: The fractionation of nitrate and DSi during phytoplankton uptake can be modelled by Rayleigh systematics

steps.action: Compare δ15N-NO3 with the fraction of nitrate remaining in AW and PSW across the seasons, finding isotope effects of 5 and 2 permil and a closed-to-open shift in PSW.
steps.quote: AW follows the traditional isotopic effect of 5 ‰ and PSW follows the particularly low isotopic effect of 2 ‰.

steps.action: Support the regenerated-nitrogen reading with particulate δ15N-PN trends reported in the supplement.
steps.quote: This is further supported by the equivalent trends observed in δ 15 N-PN (Fig. S3, Supplement S3).

steps.action: Compare δ30Si with the fraction of DSi remaining: AW fits closed-system kinetics, while PSW fits neither model; particulate δ30Si-PSi is also inconsistent with any model.
steps.quote: δ 30 Si(OH) 4 in PSW does not show a good fit with either of the fractionation models

steps.action: Revise the local reading after the misfit: PSW DSi at Fram Strait is driven by mixing and dilution, with N limitation preventing extensive DSi use.
steps.quote: DSi in PSW is not primarily controlled by biological processes

steps.action: Plot N* against δ18O-NO3 and the dual nitrate isotopes, and attribute low N* with light δ18O in PSW to coupled partial nitrification-denitrification on the shelves.
steps.quote: Water samples with lower N * are accompanied by lighter δ 18 O-NO 3 signatures.

steps.action: Reject the proposal of Varela et al. (2016) that the heavy signal comes from intermediate Atlantic-origin waters, since intermediate Fram Strait waters show no enrichment.
steps.quote: we observe no significant enrichment of δ 30 Si(OH) 4 in the intermediate water masses of Fram Strait

steps.action: Relate Δ(15–18) to δ30Si below the MLD, showing a joint gradient from AW to PSW that links shelf denitrification with removal of light Si through burial.
steps.quote: A gradient is observed between AW and PSW

steps.action: Compile published pan-Arctic δ30Si data (N. Pacific, Bering Strait, transpolar drift, Canadian Arctic, Lena River, glacial runoff), regress δ30Si on ln(DSi), and place AW, PSW and pan-Arctic trends side by side.
steps.quote: Broad negative trend lines are observed in Fig. 8, but on separate trend lines for AW and the pan-Arctic, with PSW in between.

steps.action: Reject glacial sources as a significant control, since Greenland and Svalbard glacial signatures fall off the Arctic trend in the Rayleigh field.
steps.quote: This suggests Greenland and Svalbard glaciers are not significantly impacting the Si budget of outflowing PSW at Fram Strait.

steps.action: Use the perennially ice-covered, brine-influenced Ile-de-France section (2017-2019) as a naturally found setting to test the sea-ice rival.
steps.quote: Here we evaluate the role of sea ice in influencing Arctic δ 30 Si(OH) 4 signatures in a region influenced by brine rejection.

steps.action: Reject sea-ice inputs as the cause of heavy PSW δ30Si, since the small DSi peak at about 40 m shows no isotopic enrichment.
steps.quote: Thus DSi inputs from sea ice cannot be the reason for enriched δ 30 Si(OH) 4 signatures of PSW.

steps.action: Ask what limits the complete utilisation of DSi in the Arctic.
steps.quote: This leads to the question as to what limits the complete utilisation of DSi in the Arctic.

steps.action: Plot δ15N-NO3 against DSi:N for Fram Strait together with transpolar drift, East Siberian shelf and river endmembers, revealing three mixing components rather than uptake fractionation.
steps.quote: The figure reveals the three mixing components of the Arctic N budget

steps.action: Keep the claim that widespread N limitation from rapid nitrate removal on Eurasian shelves governs incomplete DSi use and DSi export.
steps.quote: incomplete utilisation of DSi in the Arctic Ocean and its subsequent export through the Fram Strait is governed largely by widespread N limitation

steps.action: Estimate the apparent pan-Arctic isotope effect from closed- and open-system regressions, and select the open model on R² and agreement with global ε.
steps.quote: we estimate 30 ε = - 0.58 ‰ for closed system fractionation and 30 ε = - 1.09 ‰ for open system fractionation

steps.action: Check the ε estimates against independently measured isotope effects in the Canadian Arctic sector.
steps.quote: This is in close agreement with measured isotopic effects in the Canadian Arctic sector

steps.action: Infer fPSW under both models and, assuming an open system, compute the riverine (40 ± 4 %) and Pacific (8 ± 1 %) shares of the DSi inventory at Fram Strait.
steps.quote: riverine sources contribute to 40 ± 4 % of the total DSi inventory at Fram Strait

steps.action: Project that rising riverine DSi under persistent N limitation will raise DSi export to the North Atlantic and alter PSW δ30Si.
steps.quote: This implies that as terrestrial DSi inputs increase, a larger proportion of terrestrial DSi will remain unutilised

steps.action: Keep the headline claim: PSW enrichment and excess DSi trace to riverine DSi partly used and buried on Eurasian shelves under N limitation, with glacial and Pacific sources minor.
steps.quote: the increase in DSi concentration and enrichment of δ 30 Si(OH) 4 is traced to biological uptake of DSi and partial burial of biogenic Si

tree.answer: Partly; two seasons, three Ile-de-France years and pan-Arctic stations from other studies
Limited checks: standards, duplicates, independent particulate data, closed versus open model; no sensitivity test of the 40 % estimate

end.claim: Riverine DSi that is partly taken up and buried on Eurasian shelves under N limitation (from denitrification) generates the heavy, excess DSi exported in PSW through Fram Strait; glacial and Pacific sources are minor and about 40 % of the exported DSi is riverine.

decisive_move.sentence: Placing the Fram Strait AW and PSW data against a compiled pan-Arctic δ30Si versus ln(DSi) trend (Fig. 8) supports the source attribution, the exclusion of glacial sources, and the riverine-share estimate.

gates.evidence: Samples came from programme cruises (Changing Arctic Ocean JR17005, Fram Strait observatory FS2017-2019) whose stated aim was to document signatures at an unmeasured gateway, not to test a stated hypothesis. Rivals (Atlantic intermediate source, glacial input, sea ice) faced observations that could have supported them (§4.1.2 ¶5, §4.2.3 ¶2, §4.2.4 ¶1), but the headline attribution rests on consistency with fractionation trends. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Denitrifier method using the bacterium P. aureofaciens to convert nitrate for isotope analysis
MC-ICP-MS (Nu Plasma II) with standard-sample bracketing
Rayleigh fractionation systematics (closed and open system)
t-tests between water masses; least-squares regression

novelty_claims.quote: In this study, we present the first full profiles of δ 30 Si(OH) 4 measurements in Fram Strait and over the East Greenland shelf
This study provides the first full depth profiles of δ 30 Si(OH) 4 in Fram Strait
The measurement of DSi and N isotopes provides the first insights into the coupling of the N and Si cycle in the Arctic Ocean.

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the riverine share of 40 ± 4 % and Pacific share of 8 ± 1 % (§4.2.6 ¶4) are estimate_with_resolution, but the authors call this a rough estimate that assumes an open system and no net sea-ice isotopic effect; the pan-Arctic ε (−0.58 / −1.09 ‰) is estimate_with_resolution; the future increase in DSi export (§5) is an expectation with no status. The shelf burial mechanism is argued from expected sedimentation conditions, not measured, and the authors concede Barents Sea data show low burial (§4.1.2 ¶6). Deep recycling could not be quantified because of low sampling resolution (§3.3 ¶2). The paper does not report a sensitivity analysis of the source-apportionment parameters beyond the closed/open contrast (parameters are in Supplement S4, not supplied). Inference: the pan-Arctic comparison combines stations from other studies, seasons and years, with no reported harmonisation beyond depth cut-offs. The review statement names three referees, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.
